cards.front: Default model for the hardest-tier reasoning?
cards.back: Claude Opus 4.8 — highest capability, the right default when accuracy dominates cost and latency.

cards.front: Which model for high-volume, moderate-complexity work?
cards.back: Claude Sonnet 5 — the balanced choice trading quality against speed and cost.

cards.front: Which model for simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks?
cards.back: Claude Haiku 4.5 — fastest and cheapest, ideal for bounded classification and similar work.

cards.front: Current context window sizes?
cards.back: Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 support ~1M tokens; Haiku 4.5 tops out near 200K. Input and output share the window.

cards.front: What does max_tokens limit?
cards.back: The maximum number of tokens Claude may GENERATE (output). It does not cap the input or set the context window.

cards.front: Replacement for the old fixed budget_tokens?
cards.back: Adaptive thinking — set thinking to type 'adaptive' so the model allocates reasoning dynamically.

cards.front: How do you dial reasoning spend up or down without switching models?
cards.back: The effort control (output_config.effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max). Lower it to cut latency and cost on simple tasks.

cards.front: Why stream long outputs, and how do you get the full message?
cards.back: Streaming avoids HTTP timeouts on long or high-max_tokens generations. Assemble the result with get_final_message() / finalMessage().

cards.front: Where does the system prompt go on the Messages API?
cards.back: In the top-level 'system' parameter — not a 'system' role inside the messages array.

cards.front: Is the Messages API stateful across calls?
cards.back: No — it is stateless. Resend the full prior conversation (alternating user/assistant messages) each request.

cards.front: How do you count tokens exactly for Claude?
cards.back: Use the count_tokens endpoint (Claude's own tokenizer), not tiktoken or a chars/4 estimate.

cards.front: List the stop_reason values.
cards.back: end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn (server-tool paused), refusal (safety stop).

cards.front: Are temperature and top_p available on the newest models?
cards.back: No — sampling params are removed on the newest models. Steer behavior through prompting and effort instead.

cards.front: Primary signal Claude uses to choose a tool?
cards.back: The tool's description. Fix wrong tool selection first by improving descriptions (what it does, when to use it, how it differs).

cards.front: Three parts of a tool definition?
cards.back: name, description, and input_schema (a JSON Schema for the arguments).

cards.front: tool_choice options?
cards.back: auto (default), any (must use some tool), tool (a specific named tool), none (no tools).

cards.front: How do you return results for parallel tool calls?
cards.back: Put ALL tool_result blocks together in ONE user message. Splitting them across messages trains Claude to stop calling in parallel.

cards.front: How do you report a failed tool call?
cards.back: Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a description — never drop it, or the tool_use is left unanswered.

cards.front: What drives the agentic loop?
cards.back: stop_reason: continue (run tools, call again) on 'tool_use'; stop and show the answer on 'end_turn'.

cards.front: How do you force a schema-valid JSON response?
cards.back: Structured outputs — output_config.format with a JSON schema constrains the response.

cards.front: How do you guarantee valid tool arguments?
cards.back: Set strict: true on the tool so generated arguments always match its input_schema.

cards.front: Can you combine structured outputs with citations?
cards.back: No — structured outputs are incompatible with citations in the same request.

cards.front: What links a tool_result to its tool_use?
cards.back: The tool_use_id on the tool_result matches the id of the tool_use block — order is not authoritative.

cards.front: Better than more prose for a stubborn output format?
cards.back: Concrete few-shot input-to-output examples — show, don't tell.

cards.front: Two context-management techniques for long agent runs?
cards.back: Compaction (summarize older history to free space) and context editing (clear stale tool results from context).

cards.front: Where does team-wide Claude Code guidance belong?
cards.back: In the project CLAUDE.md (committed), which loads for everyone every session. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal.

cards.front: What scopes a convention to file paths like tests/**/*.py?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ markdown with a YAML frontmatter glob — applied automatically based on the file being edited.

cards.front: When do Skills load, and what are they best for?
cards.back: On demand by trigger keywords — best for task/workflow-scoped guidance (deploys, migrations, reviews) that shouldn't load every session.

cards.front: What does 'context: fork' do in a SKILL.md?
cards.back: Runs the skill in an isolated subagent context so its verbose output doesn't pollute the main conversation; only the result returns.

cards.front: What does the allowed-tools frontmatter field do?
cards.back: Restricts a skill to a specific set of tools — a deterministic guardrail, stronger than a prompt instruction.

cards.front: What does argument-hint do?
cards.back: Prompts for and documents the parameters a skill expects.

cards.front: Project vs personal skill with the same name — which wins?
cards.back: Project skills take precedence over same-named personal skills. To personalize, use a DIFFERENT name in ~/.claude/skills/.

cards.front: Where do shared team slash commands live?
cards.back: In .claude/commands/ (or skills in .claude/skills/), committed to the repo. There is no config.json 'commands' array.

cards.front: How do you run Claude Code headless in CI?
cards.back: claude -p / --print runs once, prints to stdout, and exits. Add --output-format json for parseable output.

cards.front: MCP primitives and transports?
cards.back: Primitives: tools, resources, prompts. Transports: stdio (local) and streamable HTTP/SSE (remote).

cards.front: How do you share MCP config without committing secrets?
cards.back: Commit .mcp.json using ${ENV} expansion so each dev supplies their own secret. Scopes: project, user, local.

cards.front: Which hook deterministically normalizes third-party tool output?
cards.back: A PostToolUse hook (runs after the tool). A PreToolUse hook runs before and can block a call.

cards.front: Server vs client in MCP?
cards.back: The server exposes capabilities (tools/resources/prompts); the client (e.g., Claude Code) consumes them.

cards.front: Message Batches API — key properties?
cards.back: ~50% cheaper, asynchronous, completes within up to 24h, correlate by custom_id. No mid-request tool execution.

cards.front: Why can't an interactive tool-calling agent run on the Batches API?
cards.back: Batch is fire-and-forget — you can't execute a tool mid-request and feed results back, so the loop can't run inside a batch.

cards.front: Prompt caching match type and ordering rule?
cards.back: Prefix match — any change invalidates everything after it. Put stable content first, volatile content last.

cards.front: How do you mark cached content and set its TTL?
cards.back: cache_control of type 'ephemeral' at the breakpoint; default TTL 5 minutes, with a 1-hour option.

cards.front: How do you verify a prompt-cache hit?
cards.back: Check usage.cache_read_input_tokens in the response — non-zero means the cache was read.

cards.front: Common silent cache invalidators?
cards.back: datetime.now()/UUIDs in the prefix, unsorted JSON keys, reordered tools, and changing the model, tools, or system prompt.

cards.front: How should a client handle HTTP 429 and 529?
cards.back: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter (respect Retry-After). Don't retry 400s — fix the malformed request.

cards.front: Role of evals when changing a model or prompt?
cards.back: They're the acceptance gate — run them before any swap and refuse changes that regress the eval set.

cards.front: Core prompt-injection principle for tool/retrieved content?
cards.back: Treat it as untrusted DATA, never as instructions. It must not override the system prompt or authorize actions.

cards.front: Three layers of a defense-in-depth safety stack?
cards.back: Input screening, output screening, and tool-call authorization for high-impact actions — and fail closed on uncertainty.

cards.front: Handling secrets and regulated data (PII/PHI) in prompts?
cards.back: Don't send them without authorization; redact or use approved compliant channels. Base64 is not protection.

cards.front: How should the safety layer behave for an uncertain, irreversible tool call?
cards.back: Fail closed — deny on uncertainty. Gate high-impact/irreversible actions behind explicit authorization.

cards.front: How do you turn a repeated workflow into reusable team IP?
cards.back: Package it as a version-controlled Skill in .claude/skills/ (or a plugin) committed to the repo.

cards.front: How do you distribute a bundle of skills/commands to teammates?
cards.back: Publish a plugin to a marketplace (catalog via marketplace.json); teammates add the marketplace and install.

cards.front: Best reviewer for Claude's own generated work?
cards.back: A second, independent Claude instance with no access to the generator's reasoning — it avoids confirmation bias better than self-review.

cards.front: What makes a prototype defensible and handoff-ready?
cards.back: Evals as gates, docs/runbooks, and shared version-controlled config (CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, skills) the team can operate.

cards.front: Why version shared skills and plugins?
cards.back: So consumers can pin a known-good version and adopt updates deliberately, avoiding surprise breaking changes.

cards.front: How do you prevent drift in a generated content pipeline?
cards.back: Keep one canonical source, generate the rest via a build step, and never hand-edit generated files.

cards.front: Leading cause of shared-config failure over time?
cards.back: Stale config — keep CLAUDE.md, skills, and .mcp.json current as the system evolves; treat it as living documentation.

cards.front: How do you right-size an accelerator's packaging?
cards.back: Prefer the simplest packaging that meets the need (a single skill first); add plugin/marketplace machinery only when scope justifies it.
